people/simon-kimbangu/summary: A Baptist catechist in the Belgian Congo whose healing ministry from April 1921 drew multitudes to Nkamba. Arrested by colonial authorities within months, he spent thirty years in prison in Lubumbashi, where he died. The Kimbanguist Church that bears his name became one of Africa's largest independent churches.
people/toyohiko-kagawa/summary: Japanese Christian who lived in the Shinkawa slum of Kobe from 1909, founding labour and agricultural unions and cooperatives. A prolific writer and evangelist of the Kingdom of God movement, he was imprisoned for pacifism and was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize.
people/toyohiko-kagawa/keyIdeas/0: Love in action among the poor
people/pius-ix/summary: Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, pope for 31 years (1846–78), the longest pontificate. Initially liberal, he turned against liberalism after 1848, issued the Syllabus of Errors (1864), defined the Immaculate Conception (1854) and convened Vatican I, which defined papal infallibility, as the Papal States were lost. The Mortara affair darkened his reputation.
people/pius-xii/summary: Eugenio Pacelli, nuncio in Germany and Vatican secretary of state, pope from 1939 to 1958. He guided the church through World War II — his public reticence about the Holocaust remains intensely debated alongside documented rescue efforts — encouraged biblical scholarship (Divino Afflante Spiritu, 1943) and defined the Assumption (1950).
people/c-s-lewis/summary: Belfast-born Oxford and Cambridge literary scholar who returned to Christian faith in 1931. His wartime broadcasts became Mere Christianity; The Screwtape Letters, The Chronicles of Narnia and The Great Divorce made him the most popular Christian writer of the 20th century across traditions.
people/watchman-nee/summary: Chinese Christian leader influenced by the Brethren, who founded the 'Little Flock' (local churches) movement and wrote The Normal Christian Life and The Spiritual Man. Arrested in 1952, he died in a labour camp after twenty years; his teaching shaped Chinese house churches worldwide.
people/karl-rahner/summary: German Jesuit, perhaps the most influential Catholic theologian of the 20th century and a peritus at Vatican II. His transcendental theology described humans as oriented toward holy mystery; his ideas of the 'supernatural existential' and 'anonymous Christians' reshaped Catholic thought on grace and other religions. 'Rahner's Rule' identifies the economic and immanent Trinity.
people/hans-urs-von-balthasar/summary: Swiss Catholic theologian whose trilogy — The Glory of the Lord, Theo-Drama and Theo-Logic — begins theology from divine beauty. Influenced by Adrienne von Speyr, he wrote on Christ's descent into hell and a 'hope' that all may be saved; named cardinal shortly before his death.
people/hans-urs-von-balthasar/keyIdeas/2: Dare we hope that all be saved
people/dietrich-bonhoeffer/summary: German Lutheran theologian of the Confessing Church who led an underground seminary at Finkenwalde, wrote Discipleship (critiquing 'cheap grace') and Life Together, and joined the conspiracy against Hitler. Imprisoned in 1943, he was hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945; his prison letters speculated on 'religionless Christianity'.
people/teresa-of-calcutta/summary: Albanian-born Loreto sister who in 1950 founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta to serve 'the poorest of the poor', dying and abandoned. She won the Nobel Peace Prize (1979) and was canonised in 2016; critics questioned care standards in her homes, and her letters revealed decades of spiritual darkness.
people/thomas-f-torrance/summary: Scottish theologian born to missionary parents in China, a student of Barth and editor of the Church Dogmatics in English. At Edinburgh he developed a Trinitarian, incarnational theology drawing on Athanasius and Cyril, dialogued with science, and led Reformed–Orthodox agreement on the Trinity (1991).
people/oscar-romero/summary: A conservative cleric appointed archbishop of San Salvador in 1977, who was transformed by the murder of his friend the Jesuit Rutilio Grande into a fearless voice for the poor and victims of state violence. He was shot at the altar on 24 March 1980 and canonised in 2018.
people/kenneth-hagin/summary: Texas-born Pentecostal preacher, healed as a teenager, who became the leading teacher of the Word of Faith movement through Rhema Bible Training Center in Tulsa. He taught positive confession of God's promises for healing and prosperity; critics, including Pentecostals, faulted its theology.
people/billy-graham/summary: Southern Baptist evangelist who preached in person to an estimated 215 million people in over 185 countries. He helped forge post-war 'neo-evangelicalism', founded Christianity Today and convened the Lausanne Congress (1974); he desegregated his crusades in the 1950s and advised many presidents.
people/oral-roberts/summary: Pentecostal Holiness evangelist whose tent healing crusades and pioneering television broadcasts brought Pentecostalism into American living rooms. He founded Oral Roberts University (1963), joined the United Methodist Church (1968) and popularised 'seed-faith' giving.
people/john-paul-ii/summary: Karol Wojtyła, archbishop of Kraków, elected the first non-Italian pope in 455 years in 1978. His pilgrimages to over 120 countries, support for Solidarity in Poland, theology of the body and outreach to Jews and other Christians defined his 27-year pontificate; critics fault his handling of clerical abuse. He was canonised in 2014.
people/john-stott/summary: Rector of All Souls, Langham Place, London, a leading statesman of global evangelicalism. Chief architect of the Lausanne Covenant (1974), author of The Cross of Christ and Basic Christianity, he advocated integrating evangelism and social responsibility and, tentatively, conditional immortality.
people/john-stott/place/name: All Souls Church, Langham Place, London
people/james-b-torrance/summary: Scottish theologian at Aberdeen, younger brother of Thomas Torrance, who criticised 'federal' (contract) Calvinism and stressed God's unconditional covenant of grace. His Worship, Community and the Triune God of Grace presents worship as participation through the Spirit in the Son's communion with the Father.
people/james-b-torrance/keyIdeas/1: Worship as participation in Christ's priesthood
people/rene-girard/summary: French-American scholar whose mimetic theory argues that human desire is imitative, leading to rivalry resolved by the collective killing of a scapegoat. He read the Gospels as exposing the scapegoat mechanism through the innocent victim Jesus, influencing nonviolent theories of the atonement.
people/j-i-packer/summary: English Anglican Reformed theologian, later professor at Regent College, Vancouver, whose Knowing God became a modern classic. He defended biblical inerrancy, penal substitution ('What Did the Cross Achieve?') and Puritan spirituality, and supported Evangelicals and Catholics Together.
people/jurgen-moltmann/summary: German Reformed theologian, converted as a prisoner of war, whose Theology of Hope (1964) and The Crucified God (1972) placed eschatology and the suffering of God at the centre of theology. He influenced liberation and political theologies and ecological theology.
people/gustavo-gutierrez/summary: Peruvian priest, later Dominican, whose A Theology of Liberation (1971) named the movement. He argued that theology is critical reflection on praxis in light of God's word, that salvation includes liberation from oppression, and that God shows a preferential option for the poor. The Vatican critiqued aspects of liberation theology in 1984, but Gutiérrez remained in good standing.
people/hal-lindsey/summary: American evangelist whose The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), a popular dispensationalist reading of current events as fulfilling prophecy, became the best-selling nonfiction book of the 1970s. His predictions about the generation after 1948 did not come to pass.
people/c-peter-wagner/summary: Former missionary in Bolivia and Fuller Seminary professor of church growth who coined the 'Third Wave' of the Spirit, taught with John Wimber, and later led the New Apostolic Reformation emphasising modern apostles, prophets and strategic spiritual warfare. His later teachings drew widespread criticism.
people/desmond-tutu/summary: Anglican archbishop of Cape Town and Nobel Peace laureate (1984) who led nonviolent church opposition to apartheid. As chair of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, he championed restorative justice and ubuntu theology; he later advocated LGBT inclusion.
